content: Gallaudet University was the first institution dedicated to the advanced education of deaf and hard-of-hearing individuals. It remains the only university in the world where all programs and services are specifically designed to meet the needs of deaf and hard-of-hearing students. The university is named after Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet, a prominent figure in the advancement of deaf education. Gallaudet fosters a bilingual environment where American Sign Language (ASL) and English coexist. While undergraduate students are not required to demonstrate ASL proficiency, many graduate programs mandate proficiency in sign language. In 1856, Amos Kendall, a philanthropist and former U.S. Postmaster General, became aware of deaf and blind children in Washington, D.C., who were not receiving adequate care. He had the courts declare these children as his wards and donated two acres of his land to establish housing and a school for them. In 1857, the 34th Congress passed HR 806, officially chartering Kendall’s school as the Columbia Institution for the Instruction of the Deaf and Dumb and the Blind, providing funding for the tuition of indigent deaf, dumb, or blind children from the District of Columbia. By 1864, the 38th Congress authorized the institution to grant college degrees. In 1865, the institution’s focus shifted solely to educating the deaf, and it was renamed the Columbia Institution for the Instruction of the Deaf and Dumb. In 1954, Congress amended its charter, renaming it Gallaudet College, and in 1986, it was renamed Gallaudet University. In March 1988, the Deaf President Now (DPN) movement emerged as a pivotal moment in the history of Gallaudet University and the broader Deaf community. Students protested the appointment of Elisabeth Zinser, a hearing individual, as the university’s president, following a history of hearing presidents. Alumni, faculty, staff, and students demanded that the next president be deaf. After a week of protests, Zinser resigned and was replaced by I. King Jordan, marking a significant victory for the Deaf community. In 2006, another controversy arose when Dr. I. King Jordan announced his retirement, and the Board of Trustees selected Dr. Jane K. Fernandes, the university’s provost, as the next president. This decision sparked protests from students, faculty, and alumni, both on campus and online. Critics cited concerns about the lack of racial diversity among finalists, Fernandes’ perceived lack of warmth, and her insufficient fluency in ASL. Dr. Jordan accused some critics of rejecting Fernandes because she was not deaf enough, framing the protests as an issue of identity politics. Protesters, however, argued that their concerns centered on her leadership abilities, the fairness of the selection process, and longstanding institutional issues. The protests escalated, with students blocking campus entrances and holding rallies. Despite Fernandes’ insistence that she would not step down, the university ultimately withdrew her appointment in October 2006. Robert Davila was later appointed as interim president. In June 2007, Gallaudet University faced a threat to its accreditation following the presidential controversy. The Middle States Commission on Higher Education placed the university on probation, citing deficiencies in leadership, academic rigor, student retention, and institutional integrity. The Office of Management and Budget had previously reported declining performance in key areas, including graduation rates and post-graduation outcomes. Loss of accreditation would have rendered students ineligible for federal loans and jeopardized the university’s federal funding of $108 million annually. Gallaudet University acknowledges its unique status as a federally chartered, private, non-profit educational institution serving governmental objectives. Congress has played a significant role in shaping the university, incorporating it in 1857, amending its charter in 1954, and passing the Education of the Deaf Act in 1986, with further amendments in 1992. The university receives the majority of its funding through annual congressional appropriations, overseen by the Department of Education. Athletically, Gallaudet is a member of NCAA Division III and the Capital Athletic Conference. The university’s football team is credited with inventing the football huddle to prevent opponents from reading their signed plays. In 2005, the team achieved an undefeated season after 122 years. The women’s volleyball team made history in 2006 by reaching the Sweet Sixteen in the NCAA Division III tournament, with senior Tamijo Foronda earning All-American honors. The Gallaudet Research Institute (GRI) is internationally recognized for its leadership in deafness-related research. GRI researchers collect and analyze data on the social, academic, and perceptual characteristics of deaf and hard-of-hearing populations, providing critical information for educators. The institute employs diverse research methodologies, including surveys, test norming, ethnographic studies, clinical studies, and information management.
